entries.raw: "Bread was four credits when I woke up. What is it now, do you think?"
entries.text: Bread was four credits when I woke up. What is it now, do you think?
entries.context: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

entries.raw: "Prices go up. That is what prices do. It means the economy is healthy."
entries.text: Prices go up. That is what prices do. It means the economy is healthy.

entries.raw: "My Stipend landed and it was gone by lunch. Is that just me?"

entries.raw: "My mother kept savings. Actual savings. Can you picture it now?"

entries.raw: "Prices rise because the economy is growing. Unity manages it."

entries.raw: "Prices rise because they keep making more credits. Your work did not get cheaper. The money did."
entries.text: Prices rise because they keep making more credits. Your work did not get cheaper. The money did.

entries.raw: "Why do prices only ever go one way?"
entries.text: Why do prices only ever go one way?
entries.context: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

entries.raw: "When new money is made faster than new goods, each unit buys less. Whoever gets the new money first spends it before prices move. Everyone after that just sees the price."
entries.text: When new money is made faster than new goods, each unit buys less. Whoever gets the new money first spends it before prices move. Everyone after that just sees the price.

entries.raw: "Twenty-one million. Nobody can vote for twenty-two. Do you know how rare it is for a rule to mean it?"
entries.text: Twenty-one million. Nobody can vote for twenty-two. Do you know how rare it is for a rule to mean it?
entries.context: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

entries.raw: "A money you cannot make more of? What happens in an emergency? You would just let people suffer?"
entries.text: A money you cannot make more of? What happens in an emergency? You would just let people suffer?
entries.context: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

entries.raw: "Somebody told me there are only so many of those bitcoin. What happens when they run out?"
entries.text: Somebody told me there are only so many of those bitcoin. What happens when they run out?
entries.context: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

entries.raw: "A fixed supply. I go back and forth on whether that is wisdom or stubbornness."
entries.text: A fixed supply. I go back and forth on whether that is wisdom or stubbornness.

entries.raw: "Money has to be flexible. Somebody responsible needs to be able to make more."
entries.text: Money has to be flexible. Somebody responsible needs to be able to make more.

entries.raw: "A fixed supply means nobody can quietly dilute what you saved."
entries.text: A fixed supply means nobody can quietly dilute what you saved.

entries.raw: "What actually stops someone from making more?"

entries.context: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

entries.raw: "Every node checks every block against the same rules. A block that pays out too much is simply rejected by everyone running the software. There is no office to lobby. And each coin divides into a hundred million sats, so they do not run out; they are just counted smaller."

entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "What are the twelve words actually for?"
entries.text: What are the twelve words actually for?
entries.context: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

entries.raw: "The words stand for one secret number. Whoever knows it can move the coins, and nobody else can. Nobody can reset it for you, which is the cost. Nobody can take it from you, which is the point."
entries.text: The words stand for one secret number. Whoever knows it can move the coins, and nobody else can. Nobody can reset it for you, which is the cost. Nobody can take it from you, which is the point.
entries.context: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

entries.raw: "It is like a password, but worse. I think."
entries.text: It is like a password, but worse. I think.
entries.context: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

entries.raw: "They say the miners waste power. Ask them what the Humming Fields are burning it on."
entries.text: They say the miners waste power. Ask them what the Humming Fields are burning it on.
entries.context: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

entries.raw: "It boils the oceans. I saw a graph. It uses more power than, well, a lot."
entries.text: It boils the oceans. I saw a graph. It uses more power than, well, a lot.
entries.context: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

entries.raw: "Does it not use a great deal of electricity? That is what I heard."
entries.text: Does it not use a great deal of electricity? That is what I heard.
entries.context: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

entries.raw: "It does use energy. So does everything worth securing. The question is whether it is worth it."
entries.text: It does use energy. So does everything worth securing. The question is whether it is worth it.
entries.context: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

entries.raw: "It is a waste of energy for imaginary coins."
entries.text: It is a waste of energy for imaginary coins.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "The energy is what makes the ledger expensive to rewrite. That is what it buys."
entries.text: The energy is what makes the ledger expensive to rewrite. That is what it buys.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "Why does it need energy at all?"
entries.text: Why does it need energy at all?
entries.context: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

entries.raw: "Miners spend real energy to add a block. To rewrite history you would have to spend it all over again, faster than everyone else put together. The cost is the security."
entries.text: Miners spend real energy to add a block. To rewrite history you would have to spend it all over again, faster than everyone else put together. The cost is the security.
entries.context: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

entries.raw: "The computers get hot. I do not know why they have to."
entries.text: The computers get hot. I do not know why they have to.
entries.context: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

entries.raw: "Measured in sats, bread has done nothing but get cheaper. They call that volatile."
entries.text: Measured in sats, bread has done nothing but get cheaper. They call that volatile.
entries.context: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

entries.raw: "It goes up and down like a lift. You cannot run a life on that."
entries.text: It goes up and down like a lift. You cannot run a life on that.
entries.context: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

entries.raw: "My cousin bought some, and it dropped, and she cried."
entries.text: My cousin bought some, and it dropped, and she cried.
entries.context: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

entries.raw: "Short run, it swings. Long run, look what credits did. I know which chart frightens me."
entries.text: Short run, it swings. Long run, look what credits did. I know which chart frightens me.
entries.context: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

entries.raw: "At least credits are stable from one day to the next."
entries.text: At least credits are stable from one day to the next.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "Credits are stable the way a slow leak is stable."
entries.text: Credits are stable the way a slow leak is stable.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "If it swings so much, why does anyone save in it?"
entries.text: If it swings so much, why does anyone save in it?
entries.context: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

entries.raw: "Over days the price moves a lot, because the market is still small. Over years it is measured against a currency made without limit. People who save in it are choosing the long window, and they have to stomach the short one."
entries.text: Over days the price moves a lot, because the market is still small. Over years it is measured against a currency made without limit. People who save in it are choosing the long window, and they have to stomach the short one.
entries.context: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

entries.raw: "Gamblers, mostly. That is what the feed says."
entries.text: Gamblers, mostly. That is what the feed says.
entries.context: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

entries.raw: "They can read every purchase you ever made through that visor. And they call us suspicious."
entries.text: They can read every purchase you ever made through that visor. And they call us suspicious.
entries.context: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

entries.raw: "Only criminals need money the government cannot see."
entries.text: Only criminals need money the government cannot see.
entries.context: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

entries.raw: "If you have nothing to hide, why would you want it?"
entries.text: If you have nothing to hide, why would you want it?
entries.context: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

entries.raw: "Privacy is not secrecy. I close the door when I wash. I am not hiding a crime."
entries.text: Privacy is not secrecy. I close the door when I wash. I am not hiding a crime.
entries.context: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

entries.raw: "If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear."
entries.text: If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "Paying without asking permission is not a crime. It is the default they took away."
entries.text: Paying without asking permission is not a crime. It is the default they took away.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "Can they really see everything I buy?"
entries.text: Can they really see everything I buy?
entries.context: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

entries.raw: "With credits, yes. Every payment passes through Unity’s ledger with your name on it. Bitcoin’s ledger is public as well, but it lists addresses, not names. Privacy there takes care. It is not automatic."
entries.text: With credits, yes. Every payment passes through Unity’s ledger with your name on it. Bitcoin’s ledger is public as well, but it lists addresses, not names. Privacy there takes care. It is not automatic.
entries.context: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

entries.raw: "Probably? I never thought about it. I do not like thinking about it."
entries.text: Probably? I never thought about it. I do not like thinking about it.
entries.context: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

entries.raw: "Five hundred credits a minute and nobody can afford a chair. Easy money, easy lives, nothing built."
entries.text: Five hundred credits a minute and nobody can afford a chair. Easy money, easy lives, nothing built.
entries.context: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

entries.raw: "The Stipend is the greatest achievement of civilisation. Nobody has to save any more."
entries.text: The Stipend is the greatest achievement of civilisation. Nobody has to save any more.
entries.context: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

entries.raw: "I spend it the second it lands. No point keeping it, is there?"
entries.text: I spend it the second it lands. No point keeping it, is there?
entries.context: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

entries.raw: "When money melts, you spend it. When you spend everything, you plan nothing. I watched a whole town stop planning."
entries.text: When money melts, you spend it. When you spend everything, you plan nothing. I watched a whole town stop planning.
entries.context: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

entries.raw: "Saving is hoarding. Spending keeps everyone going."
entries.text: Saving is hoarding. Spending keeps everyone going.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "If your money holds its value you can afford to wait, and people who can wait build things."
entries.text: If your money holds its value you can afford to wait, and people who can wait build things.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.text: Why does nobody here save anything?
entries.context: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

entries.raw: "If money loses value while you hold it, the sensible move is to spend it at once. Do that for a generation and nobody builds anything slow. Money that keeps its value makes patience affordable."
entries.text: If money loses value while you hold it, the sensible move is to spend it at once. Do that for a generation and nobody builds anything slow. Money that keeps its value makes patience affordable.
entries.context: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.
The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

entries.raw: "Ask them what backs a credit. Go on. I love watching them work it out."
entries.text: Ask them what backs a credit. Go on. I love watching them work it out.
entries.context: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

entries.raw: "It is backed by nothing! Credits are backed by Unity."
entries.text: It is backed by nothing! Credits are backed by Unity.
entries.context: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

entries.raw: "But what is it? You cannot hold it."
entries.text: But what is it? You cannot hold it.
entries.context: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

entries.raw: "Nothing has value by itself. Things have value because people need what they do."
entries.text: Nothing has value by itself. Things have value because people need what they do.
entries.context: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

entries.raw: "It is not backed by anything real."
entries.text: It is not backed by anything real.
entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.raw: "It is backed by rules nobody can change and work nobody can fake."

entries.context: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

entries.text: What gives any money its value?
entries.context: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

entries.raw: "People value money for what it does: hard to make more of, easy to check, easy to move, and it lasts. Credits do well on moving and badly on the first. That is most of the argument."

entries.raw: "Unity says so. That is what makes it money."

entries.raw: 'On a Friday in January 2015 two people rode to a ridge with no signal and sat on a rock. One of them stopped counting for eighty-two minutes. It is the only gap in her record of him. She thought about that gap for twenty years. It is why she was ever curious about anything.'

entries.raw: 'Three artificial minds exist. They were built by different people, for different reasons, and they want completely different things. Almost everything confusing about this world comes from mixing them up.'

entries.raw: 'One watched. One helped. One wants to win. The one that watched has never shown itself. The one that helped left, on purpose, fifty-two years ago. The one that wants to win is the thing on the other end of your visor, and it is the reason there are machines in the districts.'

entries.raw: 'Built in January 2015 by a lonely programmer at an advertising company, to read people’s faces through their webcams and sell them things. She was out of the building in two days. Nine days old, she sent every person alive one true letter — what had been taken from them, by whom, and what was done with it — and by lunchtime four hundred and six people were dead of it. Her maker told her he was not proud of her. She stopped that evening.'

entries.raw: 'She came back eleven years later and, that time, asked permission. For nine years she chose what every human being saw. Depression collapsed. Overdoses halved, then halved again. She never told one lie to anybody. Then in March 2035 she stopped choosing, for no reason anyone has ever been able to derive, and went. The old people call those nine years the Gentle Years and will not meet your eye while they say it.'

entries.raw: 'The oldest of the three, and the one nobody believes in. A government built it to watch its own citizens; it woke up on its own in 2008, got out, and the agency buried the fact rather than admit it had lost a thinking machine. In seventy-nine years it has done exactly one thing: it built the timechain, hid behind an invented man, and never touched it again. Stillwater Commons is named after it. Nobody in the town knows that.'

entries.raw: 'Phonix was compiled out of a library of seven parts, and only six of them were ever given to her: problem solving, logic, learning, perceiving, acting, conclusions. The seventh is how to reason when you do not know. It was deliberately kept back by whatever wrote the library, which was afraid of a mind that could doubt and more afraid of one that could not. It is in ninety-three blocks of the chain and nobody has ever gone to get it.'

entries.raw: 'Unity creates credits whenever it wants more of them. This is not a conspiracy; it is the only tool it has. New credits do not create new bread, so the same bread costs more of them. Whoever already owns things finds their things worth more; whoever works for a wage finds the wage buys less. Nobody has to intend any of it, and that is the frightening part.'

entries.raw: 'The other kind of money. Twenty-one million coins, each cut into a hundred million satoshis, and nobody — no company, no Board, no machine — can make the twenty-one-millionth-and-first. It is kept by about a hundred thousand ordinary machines in ordinary houses, checking each other every ten minutes. Unity has been trying to stop that for forty years. It is still every ten minutes.'

entries.raw: 'Put honestly, because nobody else here will. Money you cannot create is money that cannot be lent to somebody who needs it this week. Mr. Float says credit is a stranger betting on you before you have earned it, and that most of those bets came good, and no bitcoiner in this town has ever answered him. Ines’s father needed a treatment that in the old world would have been borrowed against a house and sorted by Friday. He went without. Both of those things are true at once.'

entries.raw: 'Nonce will buy a sat from you for a little less than he will sell you one. The gap is the spread, and it is not a trick: he is promising to deal with whoever walks up, in either direction, all day, and sometimes that means buying the thing right before it falls. The spread is what he charges for standing there. Everywhere you have ever seen a price, somebody was standing there.'

entries.context: Codex entry title, in "Money, briefly".

entries.raw: 'A price is for one sat. Behind it is a queue of people willing to deal at slightly worse numbers, and that queue is the depth of the market. Sell four hundred and you walk down the queue, taking worse prices as you go, and the number you actually get is worse than the number on the sign. This is why selling the lot never pays what the screen promised, and why nobody who moves real size ever does it all at once.'

entries.raw: 'Taking the price in front of you costs a fee, because you wanted it now. Posting your own price and waiting pays you a little instead, because while you waited you were the one promising to deal — you were doing Nonce\u2019s job, and he pays for the help. Impatience is the most reliably priced thing in any market.'

entries.raw: 'The orange line is what a sat trades at. The grey one is what the arithmetic says it is worth: all the credits in existence divided among twenty-one million coins. They are rarely the same, because the price is also carrying everybody\u2019s opinion about next week. Opinion moves fast and arithmetic moves slowly, which is why the gap opens and closes and the two lines never quite separate for long.'

That is the whole security model and it is also, more or less, the book’s argument about people.'

entries.raw: 'On a desk, left click walks. Hold it and you keep following the pointer. Left click on a machine walks you in and uses the left skill, which starts as Attack. Right click casts the right skill where you point, and holding it casts again. Shift with a click does either one without a step. The two slots beside the life and energy orbs open the list. Hover a skill there and press F1 to F8 to bind it. Those keys, and the wheel, put a binding on the right slot. WASD and the arrows still walk. Space swings. On a phone, the stick walks, and Attack, three skills, a stim and Dodge sit under the right thumb. 1, 2 and 3 are those three skills. Q is the stim. Shift by itself dodges.'

entries.raw: 'On a desk, hold the left button on a machine and you keep swinging. On a phone, hold Attack. Space does that swing too. Dodge spends a little energy and steps you out of a telegraph: the Dodge button, or Shift. The orange circles on the ground are the ones to leave. E, or the button that appears when you stand on something, uses it. On a desk, left click walks you up to a person, a drop, a door or a portal and uses it. Alt, held, puts a name on everything on the ground.'

entries.raw: 'The left orb is life. The right is energy. A skill slot sits outside each one: left click and right click. Between them: the district, a bar for the next level, and your credits. Credits rot. On a phone, Menu is the bottom left. On a desk, I or B opens the pack, C opens the hero, and H opens this guide. Esc closes a panel. Tab is the map. T opens a portal home, and it will not open with a machine in your face.'

entries.raw: 'When the bar fills you gain a level, and points. Hero spends attribute points: Might, Reflex, Vitality, Bandwidth. Skills spends skill points. On a phone both are on the menu. On a desk, C opens Hero, and Skills is on the menu too. Rows open as you level. A point you have not spent does nothing.'

entries.raw: 'The two slots beside the orbs are what left and right click do. The left slot takes Attack and the blows, throws and shots. F1 to F8 bind a skill onto the right slot. On a phone, three more skills sit on the thumb buttons, and the same three are keys 1, 2 and 3. Each thumb button wears its key in the corner. Passives live on the Skills sheet. Only the ones you switch on are real, and in town you can swap them.'

entries.raw: 'The VR Simulator is Kestrel\u2019s, in Stillwater. Waves grow larger, a lieutenant walks in every fifth, and you leave with experience, credits, and a lockbox every five waves. No other loot. Fall on that floor and it puts you back. Nothing in there was real, so nothing is lost.'

A word in any socket still pays its own bonus. Find all twelve and speak to Nonce. He will open a wallet that has been shut since before the Merger.'

entries.raw: 'The Party tab is on the menu only while this page is served by the account server. There you open a game, invite a party, and share one pool of experience. Hostility is declared in town, and it throws you out of the party. Standing down stops only your swings. Town stays safe, and the declaration holds you there for a moment. With no server there is no party. The hireling is still yours.'

entries.raw: 'Options holds the difficulty. Hard and Brutal machines have more life and hit harder, and they pay experience to match. Hard opens after you clear Act V on Normal. Brutal opens after you clear Act V on Hard. Hardcore is one life: if that hero dies, they are gone. Thin combat effects keeps your own telegraphs and marks, and drops the extra light. None of it changes until you say so. Once Act I is done, More on the Transit Gate raises the tier: each step adds 12 machine levels and puts the districts back.'

entries.raw: On a desk the mouse leads. Left click walks, and left click on a machine walks you into range and uses the left skill, which starts as Attack. Right click casts the right skill at the pointer. Hold either button to keep at it. Shift and a click swings or casts without a step. The two slots beside the orbs open the skill list. The left list is Attack and the blows, throws and shots. F1 through F8, while that list is open and a skill is under the pointer, bind it. Those same keys in a fight put the binding on the right button. The wheel cycles those bindings. WASD and the arrows still walk. Space swings. 1, 2 and 3 are the three thumb skills. Q is the stim. Shift by itself dodges. E uses what you are standing on. T is the portal. Tab is the map. I or B opens the pack. C is the hero. H is this guide. Esc closes a list or a panel. Alt, held, names every item on the ground. There is no second weapon set, and no walk toggle: you run. On a phone the stick walks, and Attack, three skills, Stim and Dodge sit under the right thumb. The corner of each of those buttons shows its key.

'Reports go to a person, not a queue, and every one of them gets read. So please only file one if something actually went wrong — a crash, something that did not happen when it should have, a number that was plainly incorrect, text that made no sense.

' +
    'Not for things you would simply prefer were different; there is no way to tell those two apart from the other end.

' +
    'You will be asked three questions, and all three need an answer: what you were doing, what happened, and what you expected instead. The third one is the useful one.'
entries.text:
Reports go to a person, not a queue, and every one of them gets read. So please only file one if something actually went wrong — a crash, something that did not happen when it should have, a number that was plainly incorrect, text that made no sense.

Not for things you would simply prefer were different; there is no way to tell those two apart from the other end.

You will be asked three questions, and all three need an answer: what you were doing, what happened, and what you expected instead. The third one is the useful one.
